event: Samuel de Champlain explores the lake and claims Vermont for France
blurb: On July 29 the explorer shot an Iroquois chief with an arquebus on the lakeshore — first contact, French style. The lake got his name.

event: The French build Fort Sainte Anne on Isle La Motte
blurb: Vermont's first European settlement was a lonely French outpost on a Lake Champlain island.

event: Fort Dummer is built — the first permanent British settlement in Vermont
blurb: Erected near present-day Brattleboro to guard Massachusetts from raids, it planted the British flag in Vermont's southeast corner.

event: Benning Wentworth starts selling the New Hampshire Grants
blurb: New Hampshire's governor issued 135 town charters in land New York also claimed — a paperwork war that eventually birthed Vermont.

event: Burlington receives its town charter from colonial New Hampshire
blurb: Governor Benning Wentworth chartered the town sight-unseen as one of his New Hampshire Grants. Nobody would actually settle there for another decade.

event: King George III awards the Green Mountains to New York
blurb: The Crown's ruling invalidated thousands of New Hampshire land titles overnight — and made outlaws of the settlers who held them.

event: Ethan Allen forms the Green Mountain Boys
blurb: The informal militia's job: run off New York surveyors and sheriffs, by intimidation where possible and violence where necessary.

event: The first permanent settlement takes root in Burlington
blurb: Eleven years after the town was chartered on paper, settlers finally put down roots on the shore of Lake Champlain.

event: The Westminster Massacre leaves two Vermonters dead
blurb: A New York sheriff's posse fired on farmers occupying the Westminster courthouse in March — weeks before Lexington and Concord.

event: Ethan Allen captures Fort Ticonderoga at dawn
blurb: With Benedict Arnold at his side, Allen demanded the fort's surrender — by one account 'in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress!'

event: Benedict Arnold's homemade fleet fights the Battle of Valcour Island
blurb: Arnold's hastily built Lake Champlain gunboats lost the battle but delayed the British invasion a full year — buying time that saved the Revolution.

event: Vermont declares itself an independent republic
blurb: Delegates at Westminster proclaimed a free state in January — first called New Connecticut. It stayed independent for 14 years.

event: Vermont adopts the first constitution to ban adult slavery
blurb: Drafted at a Windsor tavern during a violent thunderstorm, it also granted voting rights to men without property — both firsts on the continent.

event: The Battle of Hubbardton — the only Revolutionary War battle fought on Vermont soil
blurb: The rear guard covering the retreat from Ticonderoga turned and fought the British on July 7. Bennington, despite the name, was fought in New York.

event: The Battle of Bennington bloodies Burgoyne's army
blurb: John Stark's militia and Seth Warner's Green Mountain Boys crushed two British detachments on August 16 — a turning point on the road to Saratoga.

event: Thomas Chittenden becomes the republic of Vermont's first leader
blurb: The one-eyed tavern keeper governed the independent republic and then the state, more or less continuously, until 1797.

event: The Royalton Raid burns Vermont's White River Valley
blurb: Three hundred Mohawk warriors under a British lieutenant torched towns along the White River — the last major raid of its kind in New England.

event: Ethan Allen dies at his Burlington-area farm
blurb: Vermont's founding rabble-rouser died two years before the republic he helped create finally joined the Union.

event: King Arthur Flour is founded
blurb: America's oldest flour company started in Boston and moved to Norwich, Vermont two centuries later — now 100% employee-owned.

event: The University of Vermont is founded
blurb: Chartered the same year Vermont became the 14th state, UVM is the fifth-oldest university in New England.

event: Vermont joins the Union as the 14th state
blurb: After 14 years as an independent republic — and after paying New York $30,000 to drop its land claims — Vermont became the first state added to the original 13.

event: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison take a road trip through Vermont
blurb: Months after statehood, the future presidents toured the new state — officially to study botany, though politics likely rode along.

event: Thaddeus Stevens is born in Danville
blurb: The fiercest abolitionist in Congress — the radical force behind the 14th Amendment — grew up poor in Vermont's Northeast Kingdom.

event: Burlington's first newspaper, the Burlington Mercury, hits the presses
blurb: The frontier lake town got its own paper while George Washington was still alive.

event: Middlebury College receives its charter
blurb: It grew out of the town grammar school — and beat the wilderness around it to become one of America's elite liberal arts colleges.

event: Brigham Young is born in Whitingham, Vermont
blurb: The future Mormon leader who colonized Utah started life in a tiny town in Vermont's southern hills.

event: John Deere is born in Rutland
blurb: The blacksmith fled Vermont bankruptcy for Illinois, where his self-scouring steel plow broke the prairie — and built an empire.

event: Montpelier is chosen as Vermont's capital
blurb: The little town on the Winooski beat out rivals partly by donating money for a state house. It remains the least populous state capital in America.

event: Joseph Smith, founder of Mormonism, is born in Sharon, Vermont
blurb: A granite shaft at his birthplace — one foot for each year of his life — is still a pilgrimage site.

event: Runaway Pond escapes: a Vermont lake drains itself in one afternoon
blurb: Glover millworkers dug a small channel to raise their river — and the entire pond burst through, roaring all the way to Lake Memphremagog. Nobody died; the pond never came back.

event: Elisha Otis, inventor of the safety elevator, is born in Halifax, Vermont
blurb: Without the Vermont farm boy's elevator brake, the skyscraper doesn't happen.

event: British forces attack Burlington in the War of 1812
blurb: The Royal Navy bombarded the town from the lake on August 2. Battery Park is named for the American gun battery that fired back.

event: Stephen A. Douglas — Lincoln's great rival — is born in Brandon
blurb: The 'Little Giant' of the Lincoln-Douglas debates left Vermont at 20; the two rivals were both born in log-cabin country, one in Kentucky, one in Vermont.

event: Richmond's sixteen-sided Round Church is completed
blurb: Five denominations shared the one-of-a-kind meetinghouse; legend says the sixteen sides left no corner for the Devil to hide in.

event: Macdonough's fleet wins the Battle of Plattsburgh on Lake Champlain
blurb: The September 11 naval victory — partly built with Vermont timber in Vergennes — helped end the War of 1812 on American terms.

event: Emma Willard opens her pioneering school for girls in Middlebury
blurb: Unimpressed by what passed for female education, she started her own boarding school at home — a landmark on the road to women's higher education.

event: Horace Wells, pioneer of laughing-gas anesthesia, is born in Hartford, Vermont
blurb: The Vermont-born dentist first demonstrated nitrous oxide anesthesia — on himself, having his own tooth pulled.

event: The Unitarian Church is built at the head of Church Street
blurb: The brick meeting house still anchors the top of the Church Street Marketplace — the street is literally named for it.

event: The Year Without a Summer freezes Vermont crops in June
blurb: Ash from Mount Tambora's eruption brought frost and snow through the summer. The famine that followed drove thousands of Vermonters west.

event: Norwich University is founded — the birthplace of ROTC
blurb: A former West Point superintendent founded the oldest private military college in the country in Norwich, Vermont.

event: Alexander Twilight earns his degree — the first African American college graduate in the U.S.
blurb: He took his bachelor's at Middlebury College, then spent his life teaching in the Northeast Kingdom.

event: The Marquis de Lafayette visits Burlington
blurb: On his grand farewell tour of America, the Revolutionary War hero stopped in Burlington and laid the cornerstone of UVM's Old Mill.

event: The Champlain Transportation Company launches its steamboat business
blurb: It ran steamers on Lake Champlain for well over a century and was long billed as the oldest steamboat company in the world.

event: Samuel Morey patents an internal combustion engine
blurb: The Connecticut River valley inventor — namesake of Lake Morey in Fairlee — anticipated the automobile age by decades, and died in obscurity.

event: Martin Henry Freeman, America's first Black college president, is born in Rutland
blurb: Freeman led Avery College in Pittsburgh and later Liberia College — a Rutland kid who ran universities on two continents.

event: The Burlington Free Press begins publication
blurb: It started as the Free Press Weekly and is still Vermont's largest daily newspaper nearly two centuries later.

event: Chester A. Arthur is born in Fairfield, Vermont
blurb: The 21st president was born in a tiny Vermont parsonage — political enemies spread the rumor he was really born over the line in Canada.

event: 'The Torrent' — the worst Vermont flood of the 19th century
blurb: A July deluge tore through the state's river valleys, a disaster Vermonters would measure floods against for a century.

event: Thomas Davenport of Brandon builds the first American electric motor
blurb: A Vermont blacksmith and his wife Emily built a working DC motor decades before electricity had any practical use — and patented it in 1837.

event: The Fairbanks brothers start selling the world-changing platform scale
blurb: Thaddeus Fairbanks invented it; E. & T. Fairbanks of St. Johnsbury sold it to the world — scales are still made there today.

event: The Brattleboro Retreat opens as the Vermont Asylum for the Insane
blurb: One of America's first mental hospitals pioneered humane 'moral treatment' — patients farmed, bowled, and even ran a print shop.

event: Alexander Twilight becomes the first African American elected to a state legislature
blurb: The Brownington schoolmaster was the only Black state legislator anywhere in America before the Civil War.

event: Vermont's sheep population hits one million
blurb: The Merino wool craze put six sheep in Vermont for every person and stripped the hillsides bare — the deforestation is still visible in old photos.

event: Admiral George Dewey, hero of Manila Bay, is born in Montpelier
blurb: Born across the street from the State House, he became the only person ever to hold the U.S. Navy's highest rank: Admiral of the Navy.

event: John Humphrey Noyes turns his Putney Bible school into a utopian commune
blurb: The Putney perfectionists practiced 'complex marriage' until scandal chased them to New York — where they founded Oneida and, eventually, a silverware empire.

event: The Central Vermont Railway starts rolling
blurb: The iron horse connected Burlington's lumber wharves to the wider world and kicked off the city's golden age as a port.

event: National Life Insurance is chartered in Montpelier
blurb: One of America's oldest life insurers has anchored the capital's skyline — and payroll — for over 175 years.

event: The Charlotte whale surfaces — a beluga skeleton dug from a Vermont field
blurb: Railroad workers found a whale 10 feet underground, 150 miles from the sea — proof an arm of the ocean once covered the Champlain Valley.

event: Estey Organ begins manufacturing in Brattleboro
blurb: Estey became the largest organ maker in the United States, shipping half a million parlor organs from its slate-sided Brattleboro factory.

event: UVM opens its Medical College
blurb: The medical school grew into today's Larner College of Medicine, one of the oldest medical schools in the country.

event: Charles Orvis opens his fly-fishing shop in Manchester
blurb: Orvis is now the oldest mail-order retailer in the United States — it's been selling Vermonters fishing rods since before the Civil War.

event: Burlington's breakwater lighthouses first shine over the harbor
blurb: The lights marked the stone breakwater protecting what was then one of the busiest lumber ports in America.

event: The Vermont State House burns
blurb: A January fire gutted the domed granite capitol; Montpelier kept the capital only after a fierce fight over rebuilding.

event: Vermont's gold-domed State House opens in Montpelier
blurb: The third capitol on the site, rebuilt after the fire, still serves — one of the oldest working state houses in America.

event: Philosopher John Dewey is born in Burlington
blurb: America's great philosopher of education and democracy grew up in the Queen City and graduated from UVM, where he's buried today.

event: The Morrill Land-Grant Colleges Act becomes law
blurb: Vermont congressman Justin Smith Morrill's signature law created America's land-grant universities — and reshaped his home-state alma-mater-to-be.

event: Confederate raiders rob the banks of St. Albans
blurb: Twenty-one Confederates rode down from Canada on October 19, robbed three banks, and fled — the northernmost land action of the Civil War.

event: George Perkins Marsh publishes 'Man and Nature'
blurb: The Woodstock-born diplomat's book — arguing humans could wreck their environment — essentially founded the conservation movement.

event: Burlington is chartered as a city
blurb: The same act that made Burlington a city spun off its farmland as the separate town of South Burlington.

event: UVM merges with the Vermont Agricultural College
blurb: The Morrill Land-Grant Act — written by Vermont's own Senator Justin Morrill — turned UVM into a land-grant university.

event: The Cornish–Windsor Covered Bridge opens across the Connecticut
blurb: At 449 feet, the Vermont–New Hampshire span is the longest two-span covered bridge in the world.

event: The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception is built
blurb: The grand Catholic cathedral served Burlington's booming Irish and French-Canadian mill families.

event: The Tunbridge World's Fair debuts
blurb: The tiny town's agricultural fair has run nearly every year since — locals say a resident once had to be dead three days before missing it.

event: The St. Johnsbury Athenaeum opens its art gallery
blurb: The gaslit Victorian gallery, built around a giant Bierstadt painting of Yosemite, is considered the oldest unaltered art gallery in the U.S.

event: Horse-drawn streetcars are chartered for Burlington
blurb: The Winooski & Burlington Horse Railroad let Burlingtonians commute by horse-drawn rail decades before the automobile.

event: Calvin Coolidge is born in Plymouth Notch — on the Fourth of July
blurb: Silent Cal remains the only U.S. president born on Independence Day.

event: The Fletcher Free Library is established
blurb: Mary Fletcher's family fortune seeded both the city library and, six years later, the city's hospital.

event: UVM becomes the first American university to admit women to Phi Beta Kappa
blurb: The nation's oldest academic honor society got its first female members in Burlington.

event: The Howard Opera House opens on Church Street
blurb: Burlington's grandest Victorian entertainment hall hosted everything from opera to vaudeville; the building still stands at Church and Bank.

event: UVM admits African Americans to Phi Beta Kappa — another national first
blurb: Two years after breaking the honor society's gender barrier, UVM broke its color barrier too.

event: Champlain College begins as the Burlington Business School
blurb: It taught bookkeeping to Victorian Burlington before evolving into the hilltop college known for game design and cybersecurity.

event: Mary Fletcher Hospital admits its first patients
blurb: Named for the young heiress who funded it, the hospital grew into today's University of Vermont Medical Center.

event: Chester Arthur — the Vermonter nobody elected — becomes president
blurb: Garfield's assassination put the Fairfield-born machine politician in the White House, where he shocked everyone by cleaning up the spoils system.

event: The Old Ohavi Zedek Synagogue is built
blurb: Built by Lithuanian Jewish immigrants in the Old North End, it's one of the oldest surviving synagogue buildings in Vermont.

event: Wilson 'Snowflake' Bentley photographs a snowflake — a world first
blurb: The Jericho farmer rigged a camera to a microscope and spent 46 winters proving no two snowflakes are alike.

event: Rock of Ages begins quarrying Barre granite
blurb: Barre's 'granite capital of the world' quarry is one of the largest deep-hole granite quarries anywhere — and a tourist magnet.

event: Dr. Webb creates Shelburne Farms on Lake Champlain
blurb: The Vanderbilt-money agricultural estate — with barns like castles — is now a National Historic Landmark and environmental education center.

event: The Fairbanks Museum opens in St. Johnsbury
blurb: Franklin Fairbanks' 'cabinet of curiosities' — 175,000 specimens strong — still runs Vermont's only public planetarium and its longest-running weather record.

event: The Bennington Battle Monument is dedicated
blurb: At 306 feet, the stone obelisk is still the tallest structure in Vermont.

event: Rudyard Kipling builds Naulakha in Dummerston and writes 'The Jungle Book' there
blurb: Mowgli's jungle was dreamed up in a shingled house overlooking the Connecticut River valley, in the depths of a Vermont winter.

event: Fort Ethan Allen is established next door in Colchester
blurb: The cavalry post was home to the Buffalo Soldiers of the 10th Cavalry in the early 1900s.

event: Hope Cemetery is established in Barre
blurb: Italian stonecutters carved their own memorials — a granite soccer ball, an armchair, a biplane — making the cemetery a sculpture garden.

event: Battery Park is formally established as a city park
blurb: The bluff where cannons once fired on the British Navy became Burlington's sunset-watching front porch.

event: The Rutland Railroad builds its causeway across Lake Champlain
blurb: The marble-and-granite Island Line ran trains straight across the open lake; today it's one of America's most spectacular bike paths.

event: The Strong Theatre opens downtown
blurb: Burlington's early movie-and-vaudeville palace entertained the city for decades before fire claimed it.

event: Saint Michael's College is founded in Colchester
blurb: The Edmundite priests' hilltop college became one of Vermont's largest private schools.

event: Burlington Electric Department is created
blurb: The city-owned utility would, more than a century later, help make Burlington the first U.S. city to source 100% renewable electricity.

event: The steamboat Ticonderoga is launched on Lake Champlain
blurb: The last walking-beam sidewheel steamer of its kind in America ferried Vermonters for 47 years — then was hauled two miles overland to the Shelburne Museum.

event: Centennial Field hosts its first baseball game
blurb: UVM beat Maine 10–4 on April 17. It's now one of the oldest ballparks in America still hosting pro baseball.

event: The Green Mountain Club starts building the Long Trail
blurb: America's first long-distance hiking trail — 272 miles down the spine of Vermont — inspired a little copycat called the Appalachian Trail.

event: Union Station opens at the foot of Main Street
blurb: The grand rail depot on the waterfront now sports winged monkeys on its roof — a beloved Burlington oddity.

event: Cabot Creamery is founded by 94 farmers
blurb: Each farmer paid in proportion to his cows ($3,700 total) to launch the co-op whose cheddar now wins world championships.

event: The first airplane lands at what becomes Burlington International Airport
blurb: A grass field in South Burlington grew into the airport that now handles well over a million passengers a year.

event: Edna Beard takes her seat as Vermont's first woman legislator
blurb: Elected just months after the 19th Amendment, she later became the first woman in the Vermont Senate too.

event: The Champlain Valley Fair debuts in Essex Junction
blurb: The end-of-summer fair remains Vermont's biggest annual event, drawing crowds that rival the state's largest cities.

event: Vermont caps the workweek for women and children at 58 hours
blurb: Progressive-era Vermont decided 58 hours a week was quite enough — a labor landmark for the mill towns.

event: Coolidge takes the presidential oath by kerosene lamplight in Plymouth Notch
blurb: Awakened with news of Harding's death, Coolidge was sworn in at 2:47 a.m. in the family parlor — by his own father, a notary public.

event: Trinity College is founded in Burlington
blurb: The Catholic women's college educated Vermonters for 75 years before closing in 2000; UVM absorbed its campus.

event: Ira Allen Chapel is dedicated at UVM
blurb: The landmark chapel honors UVM's founder — whose statue faces the green in front of it.

event: The Bread Loaf Writers' Conference is founded
blurb: America's oldest writers' conference convenes every summer on Middlebury's mountain campus; Robert Frost was a fixture for decades.

event: The Great Flood — Vermont's deadliest natural disaster
blurb: November rains killed 84 Vermonters — including the lieutenant governor — and washed out 1,200 bridges. It remains the state's deadliest disaster.

event: The Flynn opens as an Art Deco movie palace
blurb: The Flynn Theatre premiered in the first year of the Great Depression and is now Vermont's premier performing-arts stage.

event: The Long Trail is completed end to end
blurb: Twenty years of volunteer axe-work finished the 'footpath in the wilderness' from Massachusetts to Canada.

event: WDEV radio signs on from Waterbury
blurb: The fiercely independent station still broadcasts town meeting results, high school sports, and the Trading Post — Vermont radio in amber.

event: Bennington College opens as a radical experiment in education
blurb: Founded as a women's college with no grades and required winter fieldwork, it later boasted the highest tuition in America and alumni from Shirley Jackson's circle to Bret Easton Ellis.

event: The CCC cuts the first ski trails on Mount Mansfield
blurb: Civilian Conservation Corps crews with axes created the runs that made Stowe the 'Ski Capital of the East.'

event: America's first ski tow starts pulling skiers up a Woodstock hill
blurb: A Model T engine and 1,800 feet of rope on Clinton Gilbert's farm launched the American ski industry.

event: Bromley Mountain opens for skiing
blurb: Pabst beer heir Fred Pabst built it into one of New England's first destination ski areas.

event: Goddard College is chartered in Plainfield
blurb: The experimental college pioneered low-residency education; its alumni range from William H. Macy to the founders of Phish's crew.

event: Norman Rockwell moves to Arlington, Vermont
blurb: His Vermont neighbors became the models for the Four Freedoms and dozens of Saturday Evening Post covers.

event: Hydropower supplies 90% of Vermont's electricity
blurb: Before nuclear plants and power lines from Quebec, Vermont's rivers did nearly all the work.

event: Ida May Fuller of Ludlow receives the first Social Security check
blurb: Check number 00-000-001, for $22.54. She'd paid in about $25 — and lived to 100, collecting nearly $23,000.

event: Stowe installs Vermont's first single chairlift
blurb: The American Steel & Wire chair hauled skiers 6,300 feet up Mount Mansfield — the longest lift in the country at the time.

event: The von Trapp family settles in Stowe
blurb: The real Sound of Music family chose Stowe because the hills reminded them of Austria; their lodge opened to guests in 1950.

event: Shirley Jackson settles in North Bennington
blurb: 'The Lottery' — her chilling 1948 tale of a village stoning — was written in the shadow of the Vermont village greens she lived among.

event: Marlboro College is founded on a hill farm
blurb: Built partly by returning WWII veterans, the tiny self-governing college ran on town-meeting democracy until it closed in 2020.

event: The Vermont Country Store opens in Weston
blurb: Vrest Orton's catalog-and-cracker-barrel operation resurrected the 19th-century general store and still mails its catalog nationwide.

event: Carlton Fisk is born in Bellows Falls
blurb: The Hall of Fame catcher of 1975 World Series 'wave it fair' fame is Vermont-born — Bellows Falls simply had the nearest hospital.

event: Electra Havemeyer Webb founds the Shelburne Museum
blurb: The folk-art pioneer collected entire buildings — a lighthouse, a jail, a round barn — and parked a 220-foot steamboat on the lawn.

event: The Coast Guard establishes its Burlington station
blurb: Station Burlington began on tiny Juniper Island before moving to the city waterfront it patrols today.

event: George Aiken names the 'Northeast Kingdom'
blurb: The former governor's speech gave Vermont's wild northeastern corner the royal title it still carries.

event: Andrea Mead Lawrence of Rutland County wins double Olympic gold
blurb: At 19 she took both the slalom and giant slalom in Oslo — still the only American alpine skier to win two golds in one Games.

event: Ethan Allen Air Force Base is activated
blurb: Cold War interceptor jets once scrambled from what is now the commercial runway of Burlington's airport.

event: WCAX signs on as Vermont's first TV station
blurb: Channel 3 began broadcasting from Burlington in September; Vermonters have argued with its weather forecasts ever since.

event: Consuelo Bailey becomes the first woman elected lieutenant governor of any U.S. state
blurb: The Vermont Republican blazed the trail; no woman had presided over a state senate before her.

event: Smugglers' Notch resort is founded
blurb: Named for the mountain pass where Vermonters smuggled goods to Canada during the 1807 embargo — and liquor during Prohibition.

event: Killington opens with two rope tows
blurb: It opened December 13 with trails only reachable by tractor road — and grew into the biggest ski resort in the East.

event: Robert Frost is named poet laureate of Vermont
blurb: Frost summered and taught at Ripton for four decades; his farm near Bread Loaf is now a National Historic Landmark.

event: The Morgan horse is named Vermont's state animal
blurb: Every Morgan on earth traces to one prolific stallion, Figure, owned by Randolph schoolteacher Justin Morgan in the 1790s.

event: Bread and Puppet Theater is founded
blurb: Peter Schumann's giant papier-mâché puppets started in New York and moved to a Glover farm, where the radical theater still bakes sourdough for its audiences.

event: The Northeast Blackout leaves Vermont dark
blurb: The great cascade failure blacked out 30 million people; Vermont went roughly 12 hours without power.

event: Vermont bans billboards statewide
blurb: One of only four states to do it — the reason Vermont highways still look like Vermont.

event: John LeClair of St. Albans is born — future first Vermonter NHL star
blurb: With Philadelphia's Legion of Doom line he became the first American-born player to score 50 goals in three straight NHL seasons.

event: Act 250, Vermont's landmark land-use law, is passed
blurb: The development-review law aimed to stop sprawl — and is a big reason Vermont was the last state in America to get a Walmart.

event: The first Green Up Day sends Vermonters out to clean the roadsides
blurb: Governor Deane Davis closed the interstates so volunteers could pick up litter. The statewide cleanup day has run every year since.

event: A one-day street fair closes Church Street to cars — 15,000 people show up
blurb: The experiment planted the seed: maybe downtown's main street didn't need cars at all.

event: Arson destroys Burlington's Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
blurb: A teenage arsonist burned the century-old cathedral to the ground; its modernist replacement was itself demolished decades later.

event: Vermont Yankee, the state's only nuclear plant, powers up
blurb: For four decades the Vernon reactor generated most of the electricity produced inside Vermont.

event: Vermont Law School holds its founding
blurb: Set in tiny South Royalton, it became the country's top-ranked environmental law program.

event: Patrick Leahy is elected as Vermont's first-ever Democratic U.S. senator
blurb: In the post-Watergate wave, the 34-year-old prosecutor became the first non-Republican Vermont had sent to the Senate since 1856.

event: The enclosed Burlington Square Mall opens downtown
blurb: The indoor mall — later Burlington Town Center — rose alongside Church Street during the urban-renewal era.

event: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn goes into exile in Cavendish, Vermont
blurb: The Nobel-winning Soviet dissident wrote behind a chain-link fence for 18 years; his Cavendish neighbors famously refused to give directions to his house.

event: Bill Koch of Guilford wins America's first Olympic cross-country skiing medal
blurb: The Vermonter's silver at Innsbruck stunned the Nordic world — no American had ever medaled in the sport.

event: Sandra Mansi photographs 'Champ,' Lake Champlain's monster
blurb: The famous photo of a long neck rising from the lake has never been fully explained — and never been repeated.

event: Vermont Public Radio hits the airwaves
blurb: VPR's first signal went out from Mount Ascutney that August; it merged with Vermont PBS in 2021 to form Vermont Public.

event: Jake Burton Carpenter founds Burton Snowboards
blurb: Working out of a Londonderry barn, Burton refined the 'Snurfer' into the snowboard — and built the sport's biggest brand.

event: Ben & Jerry's scoops its first cone in a renovated Burlington gas station
blurb: Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield learned ice cream making from a $5 Penn State correspondence course before opening at St. Paul and College.

event: Ben & Jerry's holds its first Free Cone Day
blurb: The pair celebrated surviving their first year by giving ice cream away — a tradition every scoop shop still honors.

event: Winooski studies putting a dome over the entire city
blurb: To cut heating bills, the city seriously researched a mile-wide dome (cars banned inside). Decades later a city planner still insisted: 'Economically, it's a slam dunk.'

event: Construction begins on the Church Street pedestrian mall
blurb: Crews broke ground on July 7 after voters approved the $6 million plan to brick over the city's main street.

event: The Church Street Marketplace is completed
blurb: The four-block, car-free marketplace opened and became the model American pedestrian mall — one of the few that actually worked.

event: The first Ben & Jerry's franchise opens
blurb: The same year, Time magazine crowned their product the best ice cream in the world.

event: Bernie Sanders wins the Burlington mayor's race by 10 votes
blurb: The socialist upset six-term incumbent Gordon Paquette by a recount-thinned margin of ten ballots — and changed Vermont politics forever.

event: Green Mountain Coffee Roasters starts brewing in Vermont
blurb: The small Waitsfield roastery grew into the coffee giant behind Keurig — for years one of Vermont's most valuable companies.

event: Phish plays its first gig in a UVM dorm cafeteria
blurb: On December 2 the future jam giants covered classic rock at Harris Millis Cafeteria — including two Grateful Dead songs.

event: John Sortino starts selling teddy bears from a cart in Burlington
blurb: The Vermont Teddy Bear Company grew from an open-air market stand into one of the state's biggest mail-order businesses.

event: Bruegger's Bagels is founded — and headquartered in Burlington
blurb: The first shop opened in Troy, New York, but the bagel chain ran its empire from the Queen City.

event: Phish begins its legendary residency at Nectar's
blurb: The band played dozens of shows at the Main Street bar and never forgot it — they later named an album after owner Nectar Rorris.

event: Ben & Jerry's opens its Waterbury factory
blurb: The factory tour became one of Vermont's most popular tourist attractions, complete with a Flavor Graveyard for retired pints.

event: Page McConnell joins Phish
blurb: The keyboardist offered to join while Trey and Fish were vacationing in Europe, completing the classic lineup.

event: Madeleine Kunin becomes Vermont's first female governor
blurb: The Swiss-born Democrat, whose family fled the Nazis, went on to serve three terms and later became U.S. ambassador to Switzerland.

event: Stratton hosts its first US Open of snowboarding
blurb: Stratton had just become the first ski area to allow snowboarding; Jake Burton's US Open made it the sport's spiritual home.

event: The Moran coal plant on Burlington's waterfront goes dark
blurb: The hulking brick generating station was left to rust on the lakeshore, launching three decades of what-do-we-do-with-it debates.

event: Cherry Garcia — the first ice cream named for a rock star — hits freezers
blurb: Suggested by anonymous Deadheads via postcard, the flavor honored Jerry Garcia and became a company best-seller.

event: Circus Smirkus pitches its first tent in Greensboro
blurb: Rob Mermin's international youth circus sends Vermont kids on tour under the big top every summer.

event: Phish tours beyond the Northeast for the first time
blurb: A seven-date run in Colorado was the band's first venture out of New England's orbit — the national obsession started here.

event: Seventh Generation is founded in Burlington
blurb: The green-cleaning company took its name from an Iroquois principle: consider the impact on the seventh generation to come.

event: Greg Noonan opens the Vermont Pub & Brewery — the state's first brewpub
blurb: Noonan spent three years lobbying to make brewpubs legal, then opened Burlington's beer landmark and literally wrote the book on brewing.

event: Outright Vermont is founded
blurb: The pioneering LGBTQ+ youth organization launched in Burlington a decade before Vermont invented the civil union.

event: Long Trail Brewing is founded in a woolen mill basement
blurb: Its Long Trail Ale — a Düsseldorf altbier — became Vermont's best-selling craft beer for years.

event: The first Vermont City Marathon runs through Burlington
blurb: The Memorial Day-weekend race became New England's second-biggest marathon, finishing on the Lake Champlain waterfront.

event: A Burlington student designs the city's first flag as a school project
blurb: Cara Wick's classroom design flew over the city for 27 years — until another school competition replaced it.

event: Bernie Sanders is elected to the U.S. House
blurb: Vermont sent the first independent socialist to Congress in four decades; he held the seat for 16 years.

event: Howard Dean becomes governor of Vermont
blurb: The physician was lieutenant governor when Governor Snelling died in office that August — Dean was reportedly giving a patient a physical when he got the news.

event: Phish releases 'A Picture of Nectar,' a love letter to a Burlington bar owner
blurb: Their major-label debut put Nectar Rorris's face on an orange — thanking the man whose bar (and fries) kept them alive.

event: The Charlotte whale becomes Vermont's official state fossil
blurb: What other state's fossil is a whale? It was later retitled the state 'marine fossil' to make room for a mammoth.

event: Magic Hat starts brewing in Burlington
blurb: Its flagship #9 'not quite pale ale' helped launch Vermont's craft beer boom.

event: Minor league baseball returns: the Vermont Expos debut in Burlington
blurb: The Montreal farm club took over Centennial Field and later became the Lake Monsters, named for Champ himself.

event: Seven Days publishes its first issue
blurb: Two reporters founded Burlington's free alt-weekly, which outlived most of America's alt-weeklies and became Vermont's biggest newsroom.

event: Phish throws the Clifford Ball, its first giant festival
blurb: 70,000 fans took over a decommissioned Air Force base on Lake Champlain — briefly one of the largest 'cities' in the region.

event: Jody Williams of Putney wins the Nobel Peace Prize
blurb: Her campaign to ban landmines, run partly from rural Vermont, won the prize and produced an international treaty.

event: Burlington's city government launches its first website
blurb: The Queen City staked its claim on the World Wide Web back when the modem still screeched.

event: The Great Ice Storm coats northern New England in ice
blurb: January's five back-to-back ice storms snapped power lines and trees from Ontario to Maine, leaving parts of Vermont dark for days.

event: Lake Champlain is briefly declared America's sixth Great Lake
blurb: President Clinton signed it into law on March 6; an amused Congress repealed the designation 18 days later.

event: Phish plays all night into the new millennium at Big Cypress
blurb: The Florida Everglades set hosted a legendary sunrise set; Rolling Stone later named it one of the 50 greatest concerts of 50 years.

event: Ben & Jerry's sells to Unilever for $326 million
blurb: The counterculture creamery joined a multinational conglomerate — with an unusual deal preserving an independent social-mission board.

event: Vermont invents the civil union
blurb: Ordered by its Supreme Court to treat same-sex couples equally, Vermont's legislature created a brand-new legal institution — a national first.

event: Front Porch Forum starts connecting Vermont neighbors
blurb: The hyper-local network — one forum per neighborhood — became Vermont's de facto town square, used by a majority of households in many towns.

event: Jim Jeffords quits the Republican Party and flips the U.S. Senate
blurb: The Vermont senator's May defection handed Democrats control of the Senate — one man from Vermont rearranged Washington overnight.

event: Kelly Clark of West Dover wins Olympic halfpipe gold
blurb: The Mount Snow rider took the first U.S. gold of the Salt Lake Games and became the winningest snowboarder in history.

event: Burlington's 'World's Tallest Filing Cabinet' is stacked on Flynn Avenue
blurb: Artist Bren Alvarez piled 38 file drawers skyward to mock decades of bureaucratic delay on the Southern Connector highway — which still isn't finished.

event: Grace Potter forms the Nocturnals
blurb: The Waitsfield rocker built a national career from Vermont bar stages — and later launched her own Grand Point North festival on Burlington's waterfront.

event: Howard Dean's presidential campaign sets up headquarters in Burlington
blurb: The insurgent, internet-powered campaign ran out of downtown Burlington and briefly made the Vermont governor the Democratic front-runner.

event: The Alchemist opens its Waterbury brewpub — Heady Topper is born
blurb: John Kimmich's double IPA started as an occasional pub offering and grew into the beer that launched a thousand hazy imitators.

event: The ECHO science center opens on Burlington's waterfront
blurb: The lake aquarium and science center anchors the transformed waterfront where rail yards and oil tanks once stood.

event: Phish says farewell at the muddy Coventry festival
blurb: Fans abandoned cars on I-91 and hiked miles through the mud to see what was billed as the last Phish show ever. It wasn't.

event: The 'Dean Scream' echoes out of Iowa
blurb: One over-amped 'YEAH!' after the Iowa caucuses became an early viral moment and helped sink the Vermont governor's presidential run.

event: 13-seed UVM stuns Syracuse in the NCAA tournament
blurb: T.J. Sorrentine hit 'from the parking lot' in overtime — the biggest shot in Vermont basketball history, called by Gus Johnson.

event: Bernie Sanders is elected to the U.S. Senate
blurb: He became the first non-Republican to hold Vermont's Class 1 Senate seat since a Whig won it in 1850.

event: Hannah Teter of Belmont wins Olympic halfpipe gold
blurb: Raised in a snowboarding family in tiny Belmont, she won in Torino and later funded charity with her own Ben & Jerry's flavor.

event: Anaïs Mitchell debuts 'Hadestown' in Vermont
blurb: The Addison County songwriter's DIY folk opera toured Vermont town halls first — thirteen years later it won the Tony for Best Musical.

event: Phish reunites at Hampton Coliseum
blurb: After nearly five years apart, the band returned with three sold-out March shows and hasn't stopped touring since.

event: Vermont legalizes same-sex marriage — the first state to do it by legislature
blurb: Lawmakers overrode Governor Douglas's veto; the law took effect September 1. Every earlier state had been forced by a court.

event: Burlington Telecom's debts sink the city's credit rating
blurb: The city-owned fiber network couldn't repay $17 million it owed City Hall, and Moody's downgraded Burlington's debt.

event: Hill Farmstead Brewery opens in Greensboro Bend
blurb: Shaun Hill's ancestral-farm brewery was soon rated the best in the world — pilgrimages to the Northeast Kingdom gravel road followed.

event: Tropical Storm Irene ravages Vermont
blurb: Mountain valleys turned into rivers on August 28, destroying historic covered bridges and cutting off a dozen towns entirely.

event: Hurricane Irene destroys The Alchemist pub — the same month its cannery opens
blurb: The flood wrecked the brewpub, but the brand-new canning line survived, and Heady Topper became the most sought-after beer in America.

event: Miro Weinberger is elected mayor of Burlington
blurb: The Democrat took City Hall after three decades dominated by Bernie Sanders' Progressive successors.

event: Burlington becomes the first U.S. city powered by 100% renewable electricity
blurb: Buying the Winooski One hydro dam pushed the city-owned utility across the all-renewable finish line — a national first.

event: Vermont is the first state to call for a constitutional convention to overturn Citizens United
blurb: The legislature demanded a rewrite of campaign-finance law — classic Vermont: small state, big swing.

event: Vermont Yankee shuts down for good
blurb: The reactor went offline at 12:12 p.m. on December 29, ending Vermont's nuclear era.

event: Bernie Sanders launches his presidential campaign from Burlington
blurb: The campaign HQ was downtown; the kickoff rally packed Waterfront Park with an estimated 5,000 supporters.

event: GlobalFoundries takes over IBM's Essex Junction chip plant
blurb: IBM paid GlobalFoundries $1.5 billion to take its chipmaking business — the plant remains Vermont's largest private employer.

event: Feds seize Jay Peak in the EB-5 fraud scandal
blurb: The SEC called the resort's $200 million investor-visa scheme a 'Ponzi-like' fraud — the biggest scandal in EB-5 program history.

event: Burlington adopts a new city flag designed by local kids
blurb: Brothers Owen and Lucas Marchessault won the citywide design contest; their green-and-blue waves now fly over City Hall.

event: Phil Scott — governor and champion stock car racer — takes office
blurb: Vermont's Republican governor has hundreds of stock car starts at Barre's Thunder Road; he kept racing while in office.

event: Burlington's downtown mall closes for the ill-fated CityPlace redevelopment
blurb: The Burlington Town Center came down for a tower project that then sat as a pit for years — downtown's biggest saga of the decade.

event: Vermont becomes the first state to legalize cannabis through its legislature
blurb: Every earlier state had used a ballot initiative. Vermont, which has no statewide referenda, did it the old-fashioned way.

event: Vermont Green FC kicks off in Burlington
blurb: The environmental-justice-branded soccer club began USL League Two play at UVM's Virtue Field and immediately led the league in attendance and thrifted-jersey sales.

event: Noah Kahan releases 'Stick Season'
blurb: The Strafford native's ode to Vermont's muddy in-between season went multi-platinum and put 'Vermont sad-folk' on arena stages.

event: Floodwaters swamp downtown Montpelier
blurb: July's catastrophic rains put the state capital's downtown underwater — Vermont's worst flooding since Irene, and for Montpelier since 1927.
